planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring at a pond margin or in a submerged aquatic basket set 0-2 inches deep, or in consistently moist garden soil away from water.

directions: Blue Arrows Rush forms a tight, upright clump of rigid, cylindrical, blue-gray stems that stay vertical without flopping, giving a strong architectural accent at a pond edge or in a bog garden. Set divisions in shallow standing water or saturated soil in full sun, where the steel-blue color develops most intensely; part shade is tolerated but softens the color and habit. Established clumps handle both permanently wet soil and brief shallow flooding, and they spread slowly by rhizome rather than aggressively colonizing a pond margin. Cut the clump back hard in late winter to remove weathered stems before new blue growth emerges in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into a submerged aquatic pot set 0-2 inches deep at a pond margin, or into consistently boggy soil; a compact scale suits small water features and containers.

directions: Curly Wurly is a dwarf, densely tufted corkscrew rush, notably more compact than older spiraling selections like 'Spiralis' or 'Big Twister', making it well suited to container water gardens, small ponds, and the front edge of a bog planting. Keep the roots constantly saturated in shallow water or waterlogged soil in full sun to part shade, since the tightly coiled stems lose their curl and quality if the soil dries out. Its small mounded habit works well tucked among taller pond marginals or displayed alone in a shallow dish garden. Remove any straight, reverted stems and trim out old browned growth in late winter to keep the curled form tidy.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into a submerged aquatic basket set 0-6 inches deep at a pond margin in full sun.

directions: Albescens Bulrush is a striking sport of softstem bulrush bearing tall, leafless, rounded stems marked with irregular longitudinal stripes of creamy white running the length of each stem, giving a paler, more luminous effect than the horizontally banded Zebra Rush. Plant divisions in a submerged aquatic basket set in shallow water at a pond margin in full sun, where the pale striping shows to best effect against darker-leaved companions like pickerelweed and cattail. It spreads by rhizome and should be confined to a container in a lined pond to prevent it from overtaking the margin, and any stems that revert to solid green should be cut out promptly to preserve the variegated clump. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and stem quality.

planting.note: Plant small divisions or plugs directly into saturated substrate or shallow water 0-2 inches deep at a pond margin, in a bog tray, or in a planted aquarium.

directions: Dwarf hairgrass is one of the smallest spikerushes, forming a very fine-textured, low, grass-like turf that spreads by thin rhizomes to knit together a dense green carpet along the shallow, saturated edges of a pond or in a bog tray. Plant small divisions directly into wet substrate or shallow standing water in full sun to light shade, and keep the site permanently saturated since the fine foliage has little drought tolerance. It tolerates both emergent growth at a pond edge and fully submerged culture, which also makes it a popular carpeting plant in cold-water and planted aquaria. Thin and replant congested patches every year or two, since vigorous colonies can quickly overrun small containers or shallow dish gardens.

planting.note: Plant tubers or divisions in heavy aquatic soil in a submerged container set 2-6 inches deep at a pond margin in full sun.

directions: Old World Arrowhead is the Eurasian counterpart to the North American duck potato, producing the same bold, arrow-shaped emergent leaves but with single, three-petaled white flowers that each carry a distinctive dark purple-black blotch at the base of the petals, distinguishing it from the plain white-flowered American species. Plant tubers or divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in a submerged pot set at the shallow margin of a pond in full sun, where it flowers through mid to late summer above the water surface. Underground stolons produce small starchy corms that have long been gathered and cooked as a vegetable in parts of Europe and Asia, and which also feed waterfowl in the wild. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to control spread and renew flowering vigor.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into a submerged aquatic basket set 0-6 inches deep at a pond margin in full sun to control the naturally aggressive spread of cattail.

directions: Variegated Cattail is a selection of common cattail with leaves striped lengthwise in cream to pale yellow, giving the familiar upright cattail form a brighter, more ornamental presence at the pond margin, and it is noticeably less vigorous and shorter-growing than the plain green species, making it more manageable in a garden pond. Plant divisions in a submerged aquatic basket in shallow water at a pond edge in full sun, which brings out the strongest variegation; stems that revert to solid green should be cut out at the base as soon as they appear to keep the clump variegated. Like the species, it produces the familiar brown, sausage-shaped seed heads in late summer that add winter interest if left standing. Divide and repot every two to three years in spring to refresh vigor and control spread within the container.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in saturated soil or shallow water up to 4 inches deep at a pond margin, wet meadow, or rain garden in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Green bulrush is a robust, clump-forming native sedge relative of wet meadows, marshes, and pond margins across much of North America, valued in restoration and rain garden plantings for its dense fibrous root system and tolerance of both standing water and periodic drying. Plant divisions into saturated soil or shallow water at a pond edge or the low point of a rain garden in full sun to partial shade, where dense, arching clumps of grass-like foliage support tight, greenish-brown flower clusters held above the leaves in summer. The seed heads provide food for songbirds and waterfowl, and the dense clumps offer valuable cover for amphibians and nesting marsh birds. Established clumps need little maintenance beyond an annual cutback of old foliage in late winter and occasional division every three to four years to prevent overcrowding.
